fact: CSU Extension says straw-colored or dead spots with dark green borders in lawns with dogs are caused by the concentrated salts in dog urine, particularly from female dogs.
quote: Straw-colored grass or dead spots with dark green borders are common in lawns where dogs are present. The concentrated salts in the urine of dogs, particularly female dogs, cause these spots.
source_label: CSU Extension PlantTalk Colorado 1503, Dog Spots

fact: CSU Extension says water is the only thing that reverses dog-urine damage to grass, and that baking soda, detergent and salt-leaching products have not proven effective.
quote: Water is the only thing that can reverse the effects of dog urine on grass. Some may suggest using baking soda, dish washing detergent, or products claiming to dissolve or leach the salts. They have not proven to be effective and will be ineffective and may compound the problem.
source_label: CSU Extension PlantTalk Colorado 1503, Dog Spots

fact: CSU Extension calls hosing each spot labor-intensive and suggests training the dog to use a designated area off the grass, such as a graveled or unplanted corner.
quote: Some dog owners follow the dog and wash the spots with a garden hose. This solution is rather labor-intensive but the idea is to dilute the urine. A better solution would be to train the dog to go to a specific area off of the grass. Perhaps the dog could use an unplanted area or a graveled area, or the corner of the property designated for the dog's use.
source_label: CSU Extension PlantTalk Colorado 1503, Dog Spots

fact: CSU Extension says spots that cannot be revived need reseeding or resodding, after the damaged spots are heavily watered with a hose for a few days.
quote: If the damaged grass can't be revived, it may be necessary to reseed or resod. If that is the case, the damaged spots should be heavily watered with a hose for a few days before reseeding or resodding.
source_label: CSU Extension PlantTalk Colorado 1503, Dog Spots

fact: CSU Extension lists high recuperative potential and good drought resistance among Kentucky bluegrass advantages, and poor to fair shade tolerance among its disadvantages.
quote: High recuperative potential and rate … Good drought resistance (can go dormant and survive long periods without water) … Poor to fair shade tolerance
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #561, Turfgrass Species Selection Guidelines (Koski, rev. January 2012)

fact: CSU Extension says homeowners found that twice-weekly watering restrictions still produced healthy bluegrass lawns.
quote: Homeowners discovered that twice weekly watering restrictions would produce healthy bluegrass lawns.
source_label: CSU Extension PlantTalk Colorado 1540, Drought Tolerance of Kentucky Bluegrass

fact: CSU Extension says buffalograss will not tolerate heavy, constant traffic and is not well adapted to small, heavily used home lawns.
quote: Will not tolerate heavy, constant traffic. Not well adapted to small, heavily used home lawns, athletic fields (soccer, football), or other situations where foot or vehicular traffic will be concentrated and constant.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #561, Turfgrass Species Selection Guidelines (Koski, rev. January 2012)

fact: CSU Extension says bermudagrass spreads by stolons and rhizomes, is considered a weed in most lawns, and is hard to eradicate once established.
quote: It can be quite invasive and aggressive because of prolific stolon and rhizome production. When found in most lawn situations, it is considered a weed. It is quite difficult to eradicate once it becomes established in a lawn.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #561, Turfgrass Species Selection Guidelines (Koski, rev. January 2012)
notes: Dog Tuff is a Cynodon (bermudagrass genus) selection per Plant Select; the CSU caution is about bermudagrass generally, not Dog Tuff specifically. Say so in copy.

fact: CSU Extension says traffic is the major cause of soil compaction, that a moist soil can reach 75% of maximum compaction the first time it is stepped on and 90% by the fourth, and that soils compact more easily when wet.
quote: Traffic over the soil is the major contributor to soil compaction. For example, a moist soil could reach 75% maximum compaction the first time it is stepped on, and 90% by the fourth time it is stepped on. … Soils are more prone to compaction when wet.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #215, Soil Compaction

fact: Plant Select describes Dog Tuff grass as very resistant to dog urine, quick to recover from heavy foot traffic and at home in full, hot sun, but not tolerant of shade.
quote: VERY resistant to dog urine … LOVES full, hot sun … RECOVERS from excessive foot traffic quickly … Not tolerant of shade
source_label: Plant Select, Dog Tuff Grass: Everything you need to know

fact: On the Colorado Front Range, Plant Select says Dog Tuff grass is not green until early June or after October 1.
quote: Not green until early June (in the Colorado Front Range) • Not green after October 1st (in the Colorado Front Range)
source_label: Plant Select, Dog Tuff Grass: Everything you need to know

fact: Plant Select says Dog Tuff does not blend with other grasses, so an existing lawn is killed first, and plugs go in from late May until July 15, with late plantings possibly not filling in until the second summer.
quote: Dog Tuff ™ does not blend well with other grasses. • Kill the lawn at least 2 weeks before planting … This grass can be planted any time from late May until July 15th. Late plantings may not fill in until the second summer.
source_label: Plant Select, Dog Tuff Grass: Everything you need to know

fact: Plant Select says established Dog Tuff may need water only every 10 to 14 days, needs mowing only for a trim look, and should never get weed-and-feed fertilizers.
quote: Water your new grass less than once a week the second year and beyond. It may only require water every 10-14 days once fully established. … Dog Tuff ™ does not require mowing unless you prefer a low, trim look. … Do not use weed and feed fertilizers as they contain these chemicals also.
source_label: Plant Select, Dog Tuff Grass: Everything you need to know

fact: Plant Select's profile says Dog Tuff is named for its durability in yards with dogs, spreads by runners, grows in clay, loam, sandy or gravelly soil, and should be kept in bounds with a border.
quote: It's named for its exceptional durability in yards with dogs. A sterile hybrid African form that spreads via runners … Soil Type Clay, Loam, Sandy, Gravelly … Prevent from spreading out of bounds with a boarder of taller perennials.
source_label: Plant Select plant profile, Dog Tuff grass (Cynodon 'PWIN04S')

fact: Plant Select says Dog Tuff is a sterile hybrid that cannot reseed, but it can spread into a neighbor's yard by runners.
quote: It is a sterile hybrid so it can't reseed into the wild environment and become an invasive weed (although it could get into your neighbor's yard via runners!)
source_label: Plant Select, Dog Tuff Grass: Everything you need to know

fact: Plant Select is a nonprofit plant program that Colorado State University helped create in 1997.
quote: In 1997, Colorado State University, … and professional horticulturists teamed up to create Plant Select—a 501c(3) nonprofit collaboration.
source_label: Plant Select, About Plant Select

fact: Penn State's Center for Sports Surface Research reports that synthetic turf generally runs 35 to 55°F hotter than natural grass, which commonly measures 75 to 95°F on a hot day and very rarely tops 100°F.
quote: Over 100° F (38° C) - very rare on natural grass – Commonly 75° to 95° F (25° to 35° C) on hot day – Less than air temperature • Generally, synthetic turf 35° to 55° F (20° to 30° C) hotter than natural grass
source_label: Penn State Center for Sports Surface Research, Surface Temperature of Synthetic Turf (presentation)
notes: Sports-field research (infilled synthetic turf); applies to the surface, not the air. Landscape turf in a yard is not measured here, so say "sports-field research".

fact: Penn State's sports-surface researchers list sunny, clear, low-humidity conditions with no clouds, from noon to 3 p.m., as when synthetic surfaces get hot, and say grass leaves stay cooler because they transpire water vapor.
quote: When do surfaces get hot? • Sunny/Clear • Low humidity • No clouds • Noon – 3:00 PM … Why don’t natural grass “fibers” produce heat? • Grass leaves transpire – Release water vapor – Evaporation causes cooling
source_label: Penn State Center for Sports Surface Research, Surface Temperature of Synthetic Turf (presentation)

fact: Penn State researchers found that watering cools synthetic turf only briefly, with surface temperatures rebounding 20 minutes after watering.
quote: Watering reduces surface temperature for a short period of time … McNitt et al., 2008 – Temperatures rebounded 20 minutes after watering
source_label: Penn State Center for Sports Surface Research, Surface Temperature of Synthetic Turf (presentation)

fact: A turf manufacturer tells pet owners to hose down every spot where the pet urinates, so the urine is diluted and washed through the drainage, and to use an enzyme deodorizer about once or twice a month for persistent odor.
quote: After picking up solids and in areas where your pet urinates, hose the spot down thoroughly with water. This dilutes the urine and washes it through the turf's drainage system. … For persistent odor control, especially in hot weather, regularly use an enzyme-based turf deodorizer. … typically once or twice a month.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide
